title: Hand-Built Integer Set
statement:
Build a set of non-negative integers without using any built-in hash set or hash map (no Set, Map, plain-object lookup tables, set or dict). Arrays and lists are allowed.

  • IntSet() creates an empty set.
  • add(key) puts key in the set. Adding a key that is already there changes nothing.
  • remove(key) takes key out of the set if it is there; otherwise it does nothing.
  • contains(key) returns whether key is in the set.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the set. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.out: [null, null, null, true, false, null, true]
examples.why: 4 and 2073 may share a bucket. Removing 4 must leave 2073 in place.
A set holds a key once. Adding 9 twice and removing it once leaves it gone; it must not be stored as two copies.

constraints: At most 100 000 calls in total to add, remove and contains
hints: Keys are bounded by 10⁶. What is the simplest structure that answers "is this small integer present"?
If one slot per possible key is too much memory, use a fixed number of buckets and send each key to bucket key % B. Several keys can share one bucket.
Each bucket is a short list of keys. add appends only if the key is missing; remove deletes it if present; contains scans the bucket.

explain.intuition:
A hash set is an array of buckets plus a rule that turns a key into a bucket index, here simply key % B for a fixed prime B such as 2 069. Two different keys can land in the same bucket (a collision), so each bucket keeps a small list and you scan it for the exact key.

Since keys are bounded, there is an even simpler option: a boolean array with one slot per possible key. It never collides but always uses memory for all 10⁶ keys, even when the set holds three. That is the same trade a browser makes between a dense array and a sparse object: memory for speed.
steps: Pick a bucket count B and create B empty lists.
add(key): look in bucket key % B; append the key only if it is not there yet.
remove(key): find the key in its bucket and delete it (swap with the last item and pop).
contains(key): scan the bucket and report whether the key is in it.
pitfalls: Appending on every add. Duplicates pile up, and one remove leaves a copy behind.
Removing the whole bucket instead of the one key, which deletes other keys that collided with it.
Choosing a bucket count with common factors to typical keys, like 1 000 for keys that are multiples of 1 000, so most keys crowd into a few buckets.

complexity.time: O(n / B) per call, O(1) on average with resizing

solutions.title: Direct-address boolean array
solutions.idea: Keys are at most 10⁶, so every possible key gets its own true/false slot.

solutions.title: Buckets with chaining
solutions.idea: A fixed prime number of buckets, each a short list of the keys that hash there.

followups: Keys can be any 64-bit integer, so a direct array is impossible. When and how would you grow the bucket array?
Replace chaining with open addressing (linear probing). What goes wrong with remove, and how do tombstones fix it?
